description: I'm an aspiring computer science student from Alexandria, Egypt, interested in web development, programming, and AI. I enjoy learning new technologies and building projects. I'm part of a team of six STEM students with different skills, from programming and design to research and more. We joined NASA Space Apps to work on a real space-related challenge and combine our skills and ideas to build something meaningful.
summary:
Astronauts living in space deal with a quiet but serious problem: without gravity, body fluids drift toward the head, and this has been linked to vision changes called SANS. A suit that gently pulls fluid back toward the legs can help, but every astronaut’s body reacts differently, so one fixed setting isn’t a good fit for everyone.

We built ORBTWIN to explore a smarter approach. It is a computer model of one person’s heart and blood pressure that learns how that person responds. When it doesn’t have enough reliable data, it says so and stays safe instead of guessing. We then simulated a suit that adjusts its own pressure, watched over by a separate safety system that can shut it down.

We tested four setups on virtual astronauts and shared the results as they came out, including the downsides. The adaptive suit reduced over-correction but sometimes ran at higher pressure for longer. We also show NASA’s Inspiration4 data (OSD-575) as separate reference evidence. ORBTWIN is a research simulation, not a medical device.
details:
What it does and how it works

ORBTWIN is a simulation of how a personalized suit could help with fluid shifts in space. It has three parts. First, a personal cardiovascular “digital twin” learns how one astronaut’s heart rate and blood pressure behave, using Bayesian fitting. When the data is too uncertain, it abstains and explains why instead of guessing. Second, a simulated lower body negative pressure (LBNP) suit adjusts its own pressure after a short calibration, and it learns that person’s profile over time. Third, an independent safety supervisor can stop the suit. It checks sensors, enforces stop rules and rest limits, and requires a signed acknowledgement to restart. We compared four setups on the same virtual astronauts: no suit, a fixed level, a generic adaptive suit and a personalized adaptive suit.

Benefits

The project gives a fair, repeatable way to ask whether personalization is worth the extra effort. Every astronaut pays the same calibration cost, so the benefit is measured instead of assumed. Safe abstention means the system never silently invents a command.

Intended impact

We want to help researchers think more clearly about tuning countermeasures for each astronaut, and to show a standard for honest reporting. Our results are mixed. The adaptive suit over-corrected less and reduced fluid pooling, but it spent more time at higher pressure, and personalization was not shown to help. We report that openly. ORBTWIN is a research tool, not a medical device, and it does not predict or diagnose SANS.

Tools and technology

Python 3.12 with NumPy, SciPy, pandas and Matplotlib for the models and statistics. Streamlit and Plotly for the interactive dashboard (parameter entry, validated results and NASA reference data). wfdb for an optional PhysioNet data reader. We also wrote self-test suites that run the models end to end. No special hardware is needed. It is software only.

What makes it creative

  • It treats “I don’t know” as a real output. Abstention is built into the design.
  • The safety supervisor is independent by construction. An automated check confirms it never imports the twin or the controller.
  • Personalization is tested fairly, and negative results are reported instead of hidden.
  • NASA’s Inspiration4 serum data (OSD-575) is shown as separate evidence, clearly labelled as not an input to the model.

Factors we considered

  • Safety first: lockouts, stop rules and rate limits.
  • Honesty about uncertainty: we use small, synthetic samples, and many constants are marked as placeholders.
  • Reproducibility: everything is seeded, and each run records a hash of its constants so results trace back to their assumptions.
  • Privacy: the app makes no outbound calls and asks users not to enter real patient data.
  • Scope: we avoided medical claims and kept the project to simulation.
